newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian woman begs parliament for right to die.
newsitem.headline: Australian woman begs parliament for right to die.

text.p: A dying woman begged Australian politicians not to quash the world's only voluntary euthanasia law on Tuesday as parliament began debate on a bill which would overturn the provincial legislation.

The 56-year-old former nurse, who does not want to be named, is one of two people who have won approval to end their lives under the Northern Territory law but fear the law may be overturned before they are ready to use it.

"I will die soon, but at least let me and those other terminally ill people in my position decide when," she said in an open letter to politicians which she read on Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Australia's upper house, the Senate, began the final debate on a parliamentarian's private bill to quash the nine-month-old law. The bill is expected to be passed, although only narrowly.
"Please listen to those of us who are terminally ill and too sick and too weak to argue," said the woman, in a shaky voice and sounding breathless.
"I do not want to end my life prematurely because of the timing of this vote."

Kevin Andrews, a leading member of a Christian morals faction within Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal Party, moved with Howard's backing to have the national parliament use its constitutional powers to overturn the law.
The Andrews Bill has already been passed by the lower house, the House of Representatives, with strong support.

But despite opposition by major political leaders, church, Aboriginal and medical groups, the Northern Territory's Rights of the Terminally Ill Act has overwhelming public support, with polls showing 75 percent of Australians back the right to die.
The former nurse, who is dying of intestinal cancer, said she was not ready to commit suicide.
"I just don't think the time's quite right yet and I don't want to be pressured by the bill," she said.

"This (vote) will put me in an impossible position as I face a particularly difficult death. The prospect of recurrent bowel obstruction with the associated pain and indignity is almost too much for me to contemplate."
The woman's doctor, leading euthanasia campaigner Philip Nitschke, said the looming Senate vote placed him and his patient in an impossible position.

"To assist her before (the vote) means that I have to really end her life on the basis of the fact that the main consideration is a vote in the Senate, not her pain and suffering. Now that's unethical," he said.
"If I wait until after the Senate vote and the law's lost ... I'm moving myself into an illegal environment -- it might be ethical then, but it's illegal."
Nitschke has assisted all four deaths so far under the law.
The law allows dying Australians who meet stringent conditions to commit suicide with a lethal pill or injection.
